towns:Calella de Palafrugell and Llafran.name: Calella de Palafrugell and Llafranc
towns:Calella de Palafrugell and Llafran.teaser: Two coves of Palafrugell, a cliff path between them, and a lighthouse on the headland above
towns:Calella de Palafrugell and Llafran.story: Palafrugell itself sits inland; its sea is three coves, and these are the two that matter most. Calella is the fishermen's one: small beaches split by rocks, boats pulled up on the sand, white houses built almost into the water. Llafranc, over the headland, is a single curved bay with a short promenade and a marina, watched from above by the Sant Sebastià lighthouse. A cliff path joins them in well under two hours. In mid-October the coves are emptying, the sea is still swimmable on calm days, and the first tramuntana days blow the haze off the Medes. Some seasonal places shut from late October.
towns:Calella de Palafrugell and Llafran.why: Come in autumn, when you can walk the whole front of Calella and hear only the boats knocking on their moorings.
facts: Go for
The walk between the two coves, a swim off the rocks, and the winter urchin season (its own calendar card)
Best hour
Early morning, before the day-trippers; again in the last light from the Llafranc side
Don't miss
Les Voltes at Port Bo (its own card under Linger) and the camí de ronda (its own card under Walks); the Cap Roig gardens are on the headland to the south
Eat
Casamar, on Carrer del Nero above Llafranc bay; dinner, book in summer

towns:Palamós.name: Palamós
towns:Palamós.teaser: A port that still works for a living: trawlers in by late afternoon, red prawns on the quay, a fishing museum
towns:Palamós.story: Most of this coast lives off visitors; Palamós still lives off its boats. The trawlers go out before dawn to the deep canyon offshore and come back in the afternoon with the gamba de Palamós, the deep-red prawn that carries a guaranteed-origin mark. The catch is sold in the llotja on the fishing quay, and next to it the Museu de la Pesca tells the story of the fleet, from sail to diesel. Each late spring the certified restaurants run the Menú de la Gamba; in 2026 the Fira de la Gamba filled the fish hall on 13 June. By October the town is back to working pace.
towns:Palamós.why: Stand on the Moll Pesquer when the boats come in: you see the prawn before any kitchen does.
facts: Go for
The working fishing port, the prawn, and the fishing museum on the quay
Best hour
Late afternoon on a weekday, when the boats unload
Don't miss

The fish auction (its own card: Espai del Peix) and the Museu de la Pesca beside it; check the museum's hours before going (Oct 2026). Next spring: the Menú de la Gamba ran 25 May to 14 June in 2026, with eight certified restaurants, and the free Fira de la Gamba on 13 June (Oct 2026); 2027 dates not yet out
Eat
La Gamba, on Plaça de Sant Pere by the harbour, for the prawn grilled

towns:Pals and Peratallada.name: Pals and Peratallada
towns:Pals and Peratallada.teaser: Two medieval villages of golden stone a few kilometres apart, with rice fields running out towards the sea
towns:Pals and Peratallada.story: Pals stands on a hill above the flat Baix Ter plain: steep lanes, stone arches, and below it the paddies that have made its name. Rice has been grown here since at least the 15th century, banned in the 19th over fears of fever from the standing water, and brought back in the early 20th, largely by Pere Coll i Rigau. Peratallada, a short drive inland, is lower and tighter, a knot of streets around a porticoed square; its name means carved stone. Both villages fill up on summer weekends. A weekday in October gives you the stone, the light and the lanes almost to yourself.
towns:Pals and Peratallada.why: See both in one morning and end with a long lunch under the arcades of Peratallada.
facts: Go for
Two walled stone villages and the rice plain between them and the sea
Best hour
A weekday morning; summer weekends and holidays are crowded
Don't miss
The walk from Pals out to the rice fields (its own card under Walks); the arcaded Plaça de les Voltes in Peratallada
Eat
Can Bonay, under the arcades of the Plaça de les Voltes in Peratallada, family-run since 1936

towns:L'Escala and Empúries.name: L'Escala and Empúries
towns:L'Escala and Empúries.teaser: An anchovy town with Greek and Roman ruins at the end of its seafront path
towns:L'Escala and Empúries.story: L'Escala is a fishing town that learned to keep its catch. Salt was its currency for centuries, stored in the Alfolí de la Sal, finished in 1697, and the anchovy trade grew from it; two old houses still work by hand, Callol i Serrats from 1847 and Solés. The Museu de l'Anxova i de la Sal, on Avinguda Francesc Macià, puts the tools and the boats on show. North of town a promenade runs along the shore through pines to the ruins of Empúries and the tiny walled village of Sant Martí. In October the beaches are empty and the town's own people are back on the benches.
towns:L'Escala and Empúries.why: Walk out to the ruins in the morning and back into town for anchovies on bread at noon.
facts: Go for
Anchovies at the source, the shore path, and the ruins at the end of it
Best hour
Morning for the ruins; midday for the town
Don't miss

Empúries (its own card under Culture); the shore walk from Sant Martí d'Empúries (its own card under Walks); the Museu de l'Anxova i de la Sal, hours change with the season, check by phone first (Oct 2026)
Eat
Anxoves Solés, on the Plaça de la Sardana, for tins and jars to take away

sources.label: Visitmuseum (Generalitat): Museu de l'Anxova i de la Sal

towns:Roses.name: Roses
towns:Roses.teaser: A wide bay, a star-shaped fortress older than the resort around it, and a five-table counter for fish
towns:Roses.story: Roses is the big beach town at the head of its gulf, and in summer it looks it. Look past the apartments. At the western edge of town sits the Ciutadella, a walled pentagon from the 16th century that encloses far older ground: the remains of Greek Rhode, a medieval monastery and the fort's own ruins, now run by the town as a heritage site. On the point to the east stands the Castell de la Trinitat. The fishing fleet still lands in the port, which is why the town's best table is a counter grilling what came in that morning. Autumn shrinks it back to size.
towns:Roses.why: Give the Ciutadella an hour: inside the walls you walk through twenty-five centuries in one field.
facts: Go for
The bay, the walled Ciutadella, and fish off the boats
Best hour
Morning at the Ciutadella; an early lunch in town
Don't miss

The Ciutadella (Espai Cultural La Ciutadella, Av. de Rhode 63): October to March listed as Tuesday to Saturday 10:00-17:00 and Sunday 10:00-14:00, closed Mondays; weekend guided visits €5, under-16s free; admission price not found, call 972 151 466 (Oct 2026). elBulli1846 at Cala Montjoi has its own card under Culture; it is closed until its 2027 season
Eat
Rafa's, on Carrer de Sant Sebastià: tiny, phone ahead, closed parts of the week

towns:Cadaqués and Portlligat.name: Cadaqués and Portlligat
towns:Cadaqués and Portlligat.teaser: The white village behind the cape, and Dalí's bay over the hill: Cadaqués has its own guide
towns:Cadaqués and Portlligat.story: Cadaqués is the whitewashed fishing village on the far side of the Cap de Creus massif, reached by one winding road over the hills from Roses, which kept it apart long enough to draw painters. Portlligat, a few minutes' walk north over the rise, is the small bay where Dalí lived and worked. Both deserve more than a stop on the way somewhere else, so they have their own guide, with its walks, coves, tables and larder. From this coast, plan at least a full day, and watch the forecast: a strong tramuntana makes the road and the cape hard going.
towns:Cadaqués and Portlligat.why: Cadaqués has its own guide; open it before you drive over the hill.
facts: Go for
The village, the bay at Portlligat and the cape beyond: all in the Cadaqués guide at /terroir/Cadaques-CapdeCreus/
Best hour
A calm day; avoid strong tramuntana days for the cape
Don't miss
Dalí's house at Portlligat (its own card under Culture)
Eat
Compartir Cadaqués, from three elBulli alumni; book in summer

towns:Girona.name: Girona
towns:Girona.teaser: The medieval city on the Onyar, its Jewish quarter and the kitchens that brought cooks from everywhere
towns:Girona.story: Forty minutes inland from the coast, Girona is a walled city climbing a hill above the Onyar river. The Barri Vell, the old town, is a tangle of stone steps and lanes under the cathedral; inside it lies El Call, the medieval Jewish quarter, one of the best kept in Europe, all narrow passages and courtyards. Along the river the houses hang over the water in ochre, rust and cream, colours chosen when the fronts were restored in 1983-84. The city also holds one of the world's most famous restaurants and a cluster of tables around it. Girona has its own guide, which tells it all properly.
towns:Girona.why: Girona has its own guide: come for a day from the coast, and stay for dinner if you have the booking.
facts: Go for
The Barri Vell, El Call and the river houses; full detail in the Girona guide at /terroir/Girona-Catalunya/
Best hour
Morning for the market and the lanes; early evening on the Força
Don't miss
The Onyar bridges (their own card under Linger)
Eat
El Celler de Can Roca (book far ahead); La Tabarra for Empordà wine on the Força; La Fábrica for coffee; Rocambolesc for ice cream; the Mercat del Lleó, closed Sundays (seen Jun 2026)

curiosities:Named on 12 September 1908.name: Named on 12 September 1908
curiosities:Named on 12 September 1908.teaser: The coast got its name in a newspaper column signed 'Pol', and not everyone accepts the credit
curiosities:Named on 12 September 1908.story: On 12 September 1908 the journalist and politician Ferran Agulló published a piece called 'Per la Costa Brava' in the Barcelona daily La Veu de Catalunya, signed with his pen name, Pol. It is the first known printed use of the name for this coast, and it meant wild or rugged, not brave. The name spread the next year, when a cruise sold as a trip along the 'costa brava catalana' put it into wider use. How much shore Agulló meant is unclear: some read it as the cliffs from Blanes to Begur, others as everything from the Tordera river to Cap de Creus and beyond.
curiosities:Named on 12 September 1908.why: Brava here means rugged: say it that way and you will sound like you read the original column.
facts: Touch it today
The article is reprinted in Marines, a collection of Agulló's sea writing edited by Pep Vila (Curbet Edicions)
Where the sources argue

Josep Pla questioned the credit and placed the name's origin at the Hotel Paradís in Fornells, Begur; the Gran Enciclopèdia Catalana dates the coinage to 1905; and the phrase was already used for a stretch of Mallorca's north coast

curiosities:The wind that plants the vin.name: The wind that plants the vines low
curiosities:The wind that plants the vin.teaser: The tramuntana has topped 200 km/h at Portbou, and it decides how every Empordà vine is grown
curiosities:The wind that plants the vin.story: The tramuntana is a cold north wind that pours off the Pyrenees and down across the Empordà, sometimes for days at a stretch. Gusts above 100 km/h are routine in a strong episode; the highest recorded at Portbou reached 218 km/h, on 29 January 2001. Growers learned to work with it. A vine left tall would be torn, so they keep it low, as a short bush tied to a stake. The wind pays back the trouble: it dries the leaves after rain and dew, so mildew and powdery mould rarely take hold, and the grapes stay small and concentrated. From now until spring is its season.
curiosities:The wind that plants the vin.why: Drive the vineyard roads on a tramuntana day and watch the low bushes take a gale that bends the cypresses flat.
facts: Touch it today
Any old vineyard of the Alt Empordà, around Vilajuïga or Garriguella, after a windy night: the vines stand knee-high on their stakes
Where the sources argue
Gust figures quoted for the tramuntana run loose; the 3Cat weather desk lists only six gusts above 200 km/h ever measured in Catalonia, three of them at Portbou

sources.label: 3Cat: Les ventades a Catalunya rarament superen els 200 km/h

curiosities:The oldest rock in Catalonia.name: The oldest rock in Catalonia
curiosities:The oldest rock in Catalonia.teaser: The cape's dark rock began as sea mud and ash more than half a billion years ago
curiosities:The oldest rock in Catalonia.story: The dark, layered rock of Cap de Creus started out as mud, sand and volcanic ash on an ancient sea floor, at the turn of the Precambrian and the Cambrian. Volcanic layers inside it have been dated to about 560-540 million years ago, and a gneiss nearby to about 553 million. Around 300 million years ago the collision that raised a mountain chain across Europe buried, heated and squeezed it into schist, and partly melted it at Tudela; bands where the rock was sheared into thin stripes run across the cape. The Gran Enciclopèdia Catalana calls it the most complete series of old rocks in the Catalan lands.
curiosities:The oldest rock in Catalonia.why: Run a hand over a shear band at Tudela: the stripes are a mountain range's worth of pressure, frozen.
facts: Touch it today
The Paratge de Tudela, on the north side of the cape, where the walk to the lighthouse starts (its own card under Walks)
Where the sources argue

The guide's old 580-540 million years has no source we could find; dated layers give about 560-540. Many texts call the schists Cambro-Ordovician, younger still. Geologists also disagree on when the shear bands formed: at the end of the Variscan collision, or much later, in the Jurassic or Eocene
curiosities:The oldest rock in Catalonia.maps_query: Paratge de Tudela, Cadaqués, Girona, Spain

curiosities:Did the vine land at Empúrie.name: Did the vine land at Empúries?
curiosities:Did the vine land at Empúrie.teaser: Local lore says the Greeks brought the vine ashore at Empúries; the archaeology points further south
curiosities:Did the vine land at Empúrie.story: Stand on the beach at Empúries and someone will tell you that wine came to Spain here, carried by the Greek traders who founded Emporion in the 6th century BC. It is a good story and a stubborn one. The digs of recent decades tell another. Phoenician merchants were trading along the Andalusian coast by the 8th century BC, and wine and the vine came with them; by the first half of the 6th century BC, local people at the Alt de Benimaquia near Dénia were already making their own. The Greeks surely traded wine at Empúries. They were probably not first.
curiosities:Did the vine land at Empúrie.why: Drink an Empordà red to the Greeks anyway: they made this gulf a wine port, even if they did not plant the first vine in Iberia.
facts: Touch it today
The amphorae and trade finds at MAC-Empúries; the site has its own card under Culture
Where the sources argue

The 'vine came in through Emporion' line is tradition. A 2025 book by Dani López and Lluís Tolosa, reported in Ara, says the Phoenicians in the south came first; the archaeologist Sebastián Celestino, via the ICAC, agrees but calls it a question under constant review

sources.label: Ara: Cae el mito, el vino no lo introdujeron los griegos de Empúries

El Temps (2002): the vine and the Phoenicians

curiosities:The Indianos of Begur.name: The Indianos of Begur
curiosities:The Indianos of Begur.teaser: When Begur's cork trade failed, its sons sailed for Cuba and came home rich enough to build palaces
curiosities:The Indianos of Begur.story: In the 19th century Begur lived off cork, and when the cork trade fell into crisis its young men left for the Americas, Cuba above all; one tally puts the emigrants at more than five hundred. Some came back with fortunes and built them into the hill town: tall houses with columned porches, painted walls and gardens behind, some modelled on the mansions of colonial Havana where their owners had lived. Josep Carreras i Frigola, who had gone to Santiago de Cuba in 1831, built the Casa Carreras. In 1870 the returnees opened a Casino for their leisure. The houses still stand along the old streets.
curiosities:The Indianos of Begur.why: Walk the streets below the castle and look up: the porches and painted façades are Havana, built with Begur money.
facts: Touch it today
The Casa Carreras and the Casino of 1870 in Begur's old centre; the town's heritage guide maps the Indiano houses. The Fira d'Indians in September is a calendar card
Where the sources argue
No source we found gives a count of the Indiano houses; the figure of 500-plus emigrants comes from the fair's tourism page, without a stated basis

curiosities:The smugglers' path.name: The smugglers' path
curiosities:The smugglers' path.teaser: The cliff path you walk for the view was cut so armed patrols could watch the coves at night
curiosities:The smugglers' path.story: The camí de ronda, the path that threads along the cliffs from cove to cove, was a patrol route before it was a leisure walk. First the carabineros and then the Guardia Civil walked it to watch the shore for boats landing contraband. The trade peaked in the hungry years after the Civil War, when Spain was short of almost everything: tobacco above all, and also coffee, sugar, medicines and luxuries such as lingerie and make-up came ashore at night. A few smugglers grew rich, and stories of bribed patrols are part of the legend. The path's name means simply the round.
curiosities:The smugglers' path.why: Next time the path squeezes between rock and sea, think of a guard with a lamp at two in the morning.
facts: Touch it today
Any stretch of the camí de ronda; the Calella to Llafranc section has its own card under Walks
Where the sources argue

The guide's old dates of 1940-1958 and its list of tobacco, penicillin and lingerie come from secondary accounts; the Gran Enciclopèdia Catalana confirms sea smuggling was strong on this coast and names antibiotics among later contraband, but we found no Costa Brava source for penicillin specifically or for those exact years

sources.label: Gran Enciclopèdia Catalana: contraban
